Imagine a classroom where you are given the space to explore and understand concepts on your own with the guidance of a teacher and the internet. Imagine the amount of knowledge which will open up if this non-traditional education style is adopted. That is exactly what Professor Sugata Mitra, a computer scientist and educational theorist, envisioned in his idea of how educational systems can become better equipped for the future.

At a time when conversations are moving more towards banning phones and social media, here’s a glimpse into the conversation I had with Sugata Mitra on various things from his works and life to his idea being implemented worldwide.

The idea began as a question of curiosity in Mitra’s mind. The question was whether all children — without knowing English or being financially stable — would be able to understand the functioning of a computer as quickly as others. This led to the ‘Hole in the Wall’ educational experiment, which was conducted in 1999 by Sugata Mitra.

Mitra embedded a free, internet-connected computer inside a brick boundary wall separating his office and a poor slum in Kalkaji, New Delhi. He wanted to know whether, without teachers or instructions, the neighbourhood children would be able to learn to browse the web and teach each other within hours.

“What the experiment showed was that groups of children using the Internet can learn almost anything by themselves, and I think young people will say, ‘What’s the big deal?’ But older people keep telling me, ‘That can’t be true because we must be required. We have to teach the children things. Otherwise, how will they learn?’” Sugata Mitra said with a laugh.

This is the core concept followed by the SOLE or Self-Organized Learning Environment method created by Mitra after the experiment. Basically, an educational approach which allows students to use internet-connected devices to explore big, open-ended questions together, SOLE helps foster self-discovery, teamwork, and independent critical thinking.

“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

body: The Central Bureau of Investigation has carried out searches at 89 locations across 20 States

The story so far: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has widened its offensive against “digital arrest” fraud rings under Operation Chakra-VI. The latest exercise targeted three major cases in which victims were coerced into transferring crores of rupees after being falsely told they were under police custody through video calls. Three accused have been arrested so far. The agency says its search operations were built on detailed scrutiny of bank records and digital account-access trails. The operation is aimed at tracing how the proceeds of crime moved and who ultimately benefited from it.

The agency carried out searches at 89 locations across 20 States . Among those arrested is accused Akash from Haryana, who received ₹1.95 crore of the defrauded funds into an account he had opened himself, moving the money onward the same day. Raja Karmakar of Kolkata has been accused of routing Rs.1.5 crore of the proceeds through his firm’s account, while Jyoti Rani allegedly withdrew part of the funds credited to her account in cash and transferred the rest onward.

The three cases at the centre of this crackdown illustrate the scale of the racket. A BITS Pilani professor was kept under a fabricated “digital arrest” for three months and defrauded of ₹7.67 crore. In October 2023, the victim was contacted by a caller claiming to represent India’s telecom regulator, warning that her mobile phone number was linked to a cybercrime complaint. Persons posing as Mumbai police, Enforcement Directorate, and CBI officials then took over via Skype, falsely linking her to the money-laundering case involving Jet Airways founder Naresh Goyal. The victim was threatened with arrest unless she cooperated.

They claimed that a police warrant had been issued against her. For over three months, she was made to report her daily movements and, believing her funds needed “digital verification”, as told by the fraudsters, the victim withdrew ₹7.67 crore through 42 transactions and deposited the money in various accounts as directed. She had also taken a loan of ₹80 lakh from banks to make the payments.

In the second case, using a similar modus operandi, a senior woman doctor in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar was targeted. She was kept under ‘digital arrest’ for over three months (March 15 to June 25) by scammers who posed as a telecom official, a police officer, public prosecutors, and a notary official. Using forged papers purportedly linked to the ED, the victim was convinced that she was under investigation. She was made to stay on constant video contact and share her live location at all times, including during travel. The fraudsters told her that assets worth about ₹20 crore needed to be “parked” pending investigation.

The victim broke fixed deposits, took loans, sold gold, and offloaded shares, transferring ₹19.24 crore to about 30 accounts. The police arrested one accused, Lalji Jayantibhai Baldaniya, whose account was also used to receive money, and suspected a Cambodia-based cybercrime syndicate link.

headline: Over ₹134 crore spent on proprietary software at premier institutes, says open source collective
body: FOSS United says the amount likely represented a fraction of public university spending on software it claims could be replaced by open source equivalents
full_body:

Indian universities and eminent technical institutes have spent at least ₹134 crore over the last five years on licences for proprietary software, the open source advocacy FOSS United said, citing responses to queries sent by the collective under the Right to Information Act, 2005.

“Institutions spend crores every year, teaching students software they will never own,” FOSS United said on a portal dedicated to mapping different higher education and research institutes’ software spending. FOSS stands for free open source software.

The spending likely represents only a portion of the overall money spent by institutes for software, used for everything from email, engineering design, assignment submission tools, electronic design automation (EDA) tools for chip design, and so on.

Sai Rahul Poruri, FOSS United’s CEO, told The Hindu that there was tension between the Union government’s push for technological sovereignty and the continued use of proprietary software by third parties that can withdraw their services at any time. “Technology sovereignty is unfortunately applied in an incredibly narrow lens, essentially as the geopolitical need of the hour, instead of applying the lens at geopolitical tech dependence across industries.”

Mr. Poruri said that the spending he cited was likely only around 15-20% of premier public institutes. “We haven’t even captured the IITs’ spending, which is likely an order of magnitude higher given their reliance on engineering software,” he said. “Based on the roughly ₹25 crore per annum figure we currently have, it’s not hyperbole to assume ₹200 crore of annual spending on software licences across the higher education industry, at the very least.” That would come out to ₹1,000 crore over a five-year period.

The Union government has put in place policies encouraging the use of open source software within the government, but in many areas proprietary lock-ins continue to guide decisions. One example is the semiconductor industry. At a press conference on the notification of the India Semiconductor Mission’s second phase on August 31, Union Information Technology Secretary S. Krishnan said the government would encourage open source frameworks like RISC V to build chips. However, the IT Ministry would continue to help startups and academia with access to proprietary platforms that are widely used in industry.

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has sought specific, point-wise reports within two weeks from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (MIB), the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Delhi Police commissioner, according to the proceedings of the case dated September 3.

“MeitY shall specifically confirm compliance with Section 19 of the POCSO Act, 2012, or, in case of non-reporting, state the reasons and identify the responsible officer/authority. The above issue shall not be left to a general or omnibus response on intermediary compliance and shall be answered specifically, supported by contemporaneous records,” the proceedings said.

The matter warrants examination under the POCSO Act, 2012, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the applicable intermediary framework, including preservation and forensic scrutiny of electronic evidence; identification of advertisers, publishers, beneficiaries and other persons involved; tracing of financial trails; identification, rescue and rehabilitation of child victims; and determination of responsibility of the concerned intermediaries and their officers, the proceedings said.

The Commission observed that Section 19 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, mandates reporting of known or apprehended offences to the special juvenile police unit or local police.

In matters involving suspected child sexual exploitation or circulation or commercial exploitation of such material, this statutory obligation cannot be substituted by internal correspondence, grievance redressal or regulatory engagement. Section 20 further prescribes specific reporting obligations, and the Act provides consequences for non-reporting, the proceedings said.

New U.S. tariffs of up to 100% took effect Thursday (September 3, 2026) on drones and certain components, as Washington pushes to lower its import reliance in an industry that China dominates.

The U.S. pressed G20 members on Tuesday to take a hands-off approach to AI regulation and avoid creating rules for the technology at a gathering of industry titans and commerce ministers in North Carolina.

The U.S. goals largely align with the thinking of the world’s biggest AI companies, ⁠nearly all of which are American. They want less regulation around the world for their rapidly growing businesses, or to shape the rules as they are written. Federal government requirements could hurt the industry’s profits if they slow the release of new models or prompt the companies to change how their products perform to address security concerns.

U.S. tech adviser Michael Kratsios, who is co-hosting the two-day meeting, advocated for countries to adopt the “Carolina Principles.” Countries that signed on agreed to avoid writing entirely new regulations for AI, and instead focus on writing rules for “novel” situations involving the technology, he told the G20 officials in a speech on ⁠Tuesday morning.

The Chinese government signed the principles, he told reporters on Tuesday afternoon. He did not provide ⁠a copy of the document. The Chinese embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first-of-its-kind policy problem,” Kratsios said in his morning speech to the delegates.
